explanation: A device needs mobile charge, and its band structure determines which electronic states can carry it. The figure separates the conduction-band edge EC from the valence-band edge EV by the bandgap Eg = EC − EV. These are electron energies, commonly measured in electronvolts (eV). An ideal bulk bandgap contains no allowed extended band states; defects can introduce additional states that need a separate model.

Each individual quantum state, including its spin label, can hold at most one electron. A spatial orbital can often accommodate two opposite-spin states. Filling an entire valence band produces no net transport current in equilibrium because the occupied states have balancing velocities. Exciting an electron into the conduction band leaves an unoccupied valence state that can move through successive electron rearrangements.

That missing valence electron is described as a hole with positive charge +q, where q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A conduction electron carries −q. Hole concentration p counts missing valence electrons per volume; conduction-electron concentration n counts electrons in conduction-band states. A hole is a band-dependent excitation, rather than a second positively charged fundamental particle.
example: An above-gap optical excitation can create one conduction electron and one valence hole. Initially Δn = Δp, although contacts, trapping and recombination can subsequently change their spatial distributions.

questions.prompt: Why does the two-electron capacity of a spatial orbital agree with the exclusion principle?
questions.hint: Include spin in the state label.
questions.answer: Opposite spins label two distinct single-electron states. Each complete state still has occupancy zero or one.

questions.prompt: What remains after a conduction electron recombines with a valence hole?
questions.answer: The valence vacancy is filled and the conduction excitation disappears. Energy is transferred to light, lattice vibrations or another carrier, depending on the mechanism.

title: Fermi–Dirac occupation
heading: Occupation probability must be combined with available states
problem: how the Fermi level and thermal broadening determine state occupation
explanation: To predict charge population, first ask whether a state exists and then whether it is occupied. At thermal equilibrium the expected electron occupation of an available state of energy E is f(E) = 1/{1 + exp[(E − EF)/(kBT)]}. EF is the chemical potential, kB is Boltzmann’s constant, and T is absolute temperature in kelvin. E, EF and kBT must use the same energy unit.

The energy zero is a choice of ruler. Adding the same constant to E and EF leaves E − EF unchanged, so the occupation probability stays the same. When comparing two positions in a connected device, use one common energy reference. At each position, the local separation EC − EF sets the equilibrium conduction-band population; the material bandgap EC − EV describes a different separation.

At finite temperature f(EF) = 1/2, and the transition spans an energy scale of a few kBT. A Fermi level within a bandgap remains a useful chemical potential even though no bulk band state exists at that exact energy. In the zero-temperature limit the distribution becomes a step: allowed states below EF are occupied and those above it are empty.

High above EF, where E − EF is several kBT, f(E) approaches exp[−(E − EF)/(kBT)], the Boltzmann tail. This approximation enables familiar exponential carrier formulas. Carrier density still requires a density-of-states integral; a probability by itself has no units of carriers per volume.
example: At E = EF + 2kBT, the exact occupation is 1/(1 + e²) ≈ 0.119. The Boltzmann value e⁻² ≈ 0.135 already shows a visible approximation error.

questions.prompt: Does f(EF) = 1/2 imply a half-occupied band state when EF lies in a gap?
questions.hint: Separate available states from their occupation.
questions.answer: The formula assigns a probability conditional on a state existing. An ideal gap has zero band DOS, so it contributes no band carriers at EF.

title: Density of states
heading: Dimensionality changes how available states accumulate with energy
problem: how one-, two- and three-dimensional bands supply different numbers of states
explanation: Confinement changes carrier population even before occupation is considered. The density of states g(E) counts allowed states per energy and per length, area or volume. For a parabolic dispersion with an isolated subband edge E0, g(E) scales as (E − E0)^(d/2 − 1) in dimension d. The figure uses separate normalizations to compare shapes: an ideal 1D edge has an integrable inverse-square-root singularity, a 2D subband adds a step, and a 3D band rises as a square root.

For an isotropic 3D parabolic band, g3D(E) = [gs gv/(4π²)](2md/ℏ²)^(3/2)√(E − EC) for E ≥ EC. gs counts spin states, gv counts equivalent valleys, md is the single-valley DOS mass in kg, and ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π. With joule energies this gives states/(J·m³). A 2D subband beginning at Ej instead has g2D(E) = gs gv md/(2πℏ²) above Ej, in states/(J·m²). A valley factor must appear exactly once; an effective mass that already incorporates valleys uses a different convention.

Multiply DOS by Fermi occupation and integrate to obtain density: n = ∫ g3D(E)f(E)dE, or sheet density ns = Σj∫ g2D,j(E)f(E)dE. The latter is per area, so it cannot be substituted for a volume density without a spatial distribution or thickness model. To convert SI DOS per joule per m^d to DOS per eV per cm^d, multiply by q/100^d. Finite broadening or finite plotting resolution regularizes an ideal 1D edge.
example: If two independent equivalent valleys have the same band edge and mass, their DOS contributions add. At fixed EF and T, doubling valley degeneracy doubles the carrier density contributed by those valleys.

questions.prompt: Why does a second occupied 2D subband add another DOS step?
questions.hint: Count independent sets of in-plane states.
questions.answer: Each subband has its own constant in-plane DOS above its edge. Their contributions sum, so crossing a new edge adds its step.

questions.prompt: What units distinguish a 2D carrier density from a 3D density?
questions.answer: A 2D density is carriers per area, such as cm⁻²; a 3D density is carriers per volume, such as cm⁻³.

title: Effective mass and valleys
heading: Band curvature controls acceleration and state counting in different ways
problem: why a flatter band gives a larger inertial response mass
explanation: The periodic crystal changes an electron’s response to a force. For a wave packet in a single band, group velocity is v = (1/ℏ)∇kE and its wave vector obeys ℏ dk/dt = F. Near a parabolic minimum in one direction, E(k) = E0 + ℏ²k²/(2m*), so 1/m* = (1/ℏ²)d²E/dk². The steeper-curvature band in the figure therefore has the smaller effective mass.

Real valleys can be ellipsoidal. Principal masses mx, my and mz define E − E0 = (ℏ²/2)(kx²/mx + ky²/my + kz²/mz). The single-valley DOS mass is md = (mx my mz)^(1/3); it summarizes the ellipsoid’s state count. Transport along an applied field instead samples directional masses and scattering. A DOS mass and a conductivity mass therefore need not be equal.

Equivalent conduction minima are called valleys. Their multiplicity enters the total DOS, while their orientation affects directional transport. Effective-mass approximations apply over the band region where the chosen expansion is accurate. They require revision for strongly nonparabolic bands, band crossings or low-energy Dirac dispersions.

For a silicon well with a (100) surface, the six bulk conduction valleys separate into two with their long axes normal to the surface and four with those axes in the plane. The normal effective mass sets confinement energies, while the in-plane masses affect state counting and transport. Different confinement energies redistribute the valley populations. Valley multiplicity and the two electron spin states are counted separately.
example: If the curvature in one direction is halved while a parabolic approximation remains valid, the effective mass in that direction doubles. At equal force and equal scattering conditions, the acceleration in that direction halves.

questions.prompt: Can one number always describe both DOS and directional mobility?
questions.hint: Compare ellipsoid volume with acceleration along one axis.
questions.answer: An anisotropic valley has different principal masses. DOS depends on their geometric product, while directional acceleration and mobility depend on the relevant direction and scattering.

title: Intrinsic density and mass action
heading: Bandgap and occupation set the equilibrium carrier product
problem: why shifting the equilibrium Fermi level trades electrons for holes
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" viewBox="0 0 900 500"><title id="title">Bandgap and occupation set the equilibrium carrier product</title><desc id="desc">Figure showing why shifting the equilibrium Fermi level trades electrons for holes.</desc><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z" fill="#17343d"/></marker></defs><rect width="900" height="500" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui,sans-serif"><text x="450" y="40" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">Equilibrium population product at fixed temperature</text><rect x="70" y="130" width="300" height="110" rx="5" fill="#edf4f1" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="220.0" y="192.0" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">n → 10n</text><rect x="530" y="130" width="300" height="110" rx="5" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#9a6a15" stroke-width="2"/><text x="680.0" y="192.0" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">p → p/10</text><line x1="380" y1="185" x2="520" y2="185" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="450" y="300" fill="#176a70" font-size="32" text-anchor="middle">np = ni²</text><text x="450" y="355" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">n = NC exp[−(EC − EF)/kBT]</text><text x="450" y="398" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">p = NV exp[−(EF − EV)/kBT]</text><text x="450" y="463" fill="#627b82" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle">Thermal equilibrium, nondegenerate carriers; ni depends on T.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A bandgap suppresses thermally excited carriers, while available states and thermal occupation determine how many remain. For nondegenerate equilibrium carriers, n = NC exp[−(EC − EF)/(kBT)] and p = NV exp[−(EF − EV)/(kBT)]. NC and NV are effective densities of states with units of concentration, not dopant concentrations.

Multiplying the two formulas eliminates EF: np = NCNV exp[−Eg/(kBT)] = ni². Thus ni = √(NCNV)exp[−Eg/(2kBT)] is the intrinsic concentration, with n = p = ni in a pure equilibrium bulk. For a single isotropic parabolic conduction band, NC = gs gv[md kBT/(2πℏ²)]^(3/2), provided the degeneracy factors have not already been absorbed into md.

At fixed material and temperature, increasing equilibrium electron population decreases hole population according to p = ni²/n. Temperature changes both effective DOS and the gap-dependent exponential, so ni must be recomputed. Under injection, separate quasi-Fermi levels can replace the equilibrium mass-action relation; under degeneracy, full Fermi integrals replace the Boltzmann formulas.
example: For a hypothetical semiconductor at one fixed temperature with ni = 4 × 10⁹ cm⁻³ and n = 8 × 10¹⁴ cm⁻³, the nondegenerate equilibrium model gives p = 2 × 10⁴ cm⁻³.

questions.prompt: At fixed temperature, what happens to p when equilibrium n triples?
questions.answer: Within the nondegenerate equilibrium model, p becomes one third of its original value because np = ni².

title: Dopants and neutrality
heading: Ionization and charge balance determine the mobile carrier population
problem: which fixed and mobile charges must balance in a neutral bulk
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" viewBox="0 0 900 500"><title id="title">Ionization and charge balance determine the mobile carrier population</title><desc id="desc">Figure showing which fixed and mobile charges must balance in a neutral bulk.</desc><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z" fill="#17343d"/></marker></defs><rect width="900" height="500" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui,sans-serif"><text x="450" y="40" fill="#17343d" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle">Count fixed ions and mobile carriers</text><rect x="80" y="100" width="330" height="265" rx="5" fill="#edf4f1" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="490" y="100" width="330" height="265" rx="5" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#9a6a15" stroke-width="2"/><text x="245" y="140" fill="#176a70" font-size="22" text-anchor="middle">Negative charge</text><text x="655" y="140" fill="#9a6a15" font-size="22" text-anchor="middle">Positive charge</text><text x="245" y="205" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Electrons: n</text><text x="245" y="265" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Ionized acceptors: NA−</text><text x="655" y="205" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Holes: p</text><text x="655" y="265" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Ionized donors: ND+</text><text x="450" y="415" fill="#17343d" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">n + NA− = p + ND+</text><text x="450" y="468" fill="#627b82" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle">Neutral dopants contribute no fixed ion charge; ionization depends on T and EF.</text></g></svg>
explanation: Chemical doping counts impurity atoms, while electrical neutrality counts charges. Let ND and NA be total donor and acceptor concentrations. ND+ and NA− denote their ionized populations. A neutral homogeneous bulk satisfies n + NA− = p + ND+, since electrons and ionized acceptors contribute negative charge and holes and ionized donors contribute positive charge.

Complete ionization is an approximation, often useful for shallow dopants over an appropriate temperature and doping range. Then n − p = ND − NA, and equilibrium nondegenerate mass action supplies np = ni². Both equations are needed to determine n and p. Compensation matters: the net majority population can be far below either chemical dopant concentration.

At low temperature some carriers remain bound to dopants, producing freeze-out. Ionized populations then depend on dopant-level occupation, EF and T, and must be solved together with neutrality. At high temperature intrinsic carriers can dominate. Heavy doping may introduce degeneracy, impurity-band effects and bandgap changes, requiring a material-specific model.

A shallow donor can ionize readily even when its binding energy is somewhat larger than kBT. Thermal energy and the large number of available conduction-band states act together: there are many possible extended states for the released electron to occupy. Dopant occupation, available states and charge neutrality determine the balance. Complete ionization is the useful limit of that balance over a suitable temperature and concentration range.

A quasi-neutral region can carry current. Its positive and negative charge densities remain nearly balanced while carriers move through it. Steady current therefore fits naturally with a nearly neutral bulk, while junction depletion layers and MOS surface charge require the spatial charge density in Poisson’s equation.
example: If fully ionized donors outnumber fully ionized acceptors by a factor of two, their difference supplies the net electron-minus-hole concentration. When that difference is much larger than ni, n is approximately ND − NA; the remaining holes follow equilibrium mass action.

questions.prompt: Why can n ≈ ND fail even when all donors are ionized?
questions.answer: Compensating acceptors reduce the net donor charge; intrinsic holes can also be appreciable. Full neutrality includes both carrier populations and both ionized dopant populations.

questions.prompt: Does a neutral donor contribute to ND+?
questions.hint: Distinguish the chemical total from the charged subset.
questions.answer: A neutral donor belongs to ND but not ND+. Only its ionized positive charge enters the fixed donor-charge term.

title: Degenerate carrier statistics
heading: Occupation saturation limits the Boltzmann approximation
problem: where the exponential tail ceases to represent an occupied band
explanation: Highly occupied bands require the full Fermi–Dirac distribution. For a nondegenerate conduction band, EC lies sufficiently above EF that f(E) is small throughout the important occupied energies. Once EF approaches or enters the band, exclusion limits each spin state’s occupation to one and the exponential approximation loses accuracy.

The reliable general expression is n = ∫EC∞ g(E)/{1 + exp[(E − EF)/(kBT)]} dE. For a parabolic band this can be expressed as a Fermi integral, with its normalization stated explicitly. The figure compares edge occupations rather than integrated carrier densities; it reveals why a Boltzmann prediction above unity cannot describe a state probability.

There is no universal dopant concentration at which every material becomes degenerate. The relevant criterion depends on EF relative to the band edge, the DOS, temperature and ionization. Very heavy doping can additionally alter the band structure through disorder and many-body effects. Those changes are distinct from using the correct occupation distribution for a fixed band.
example: At EF = EC the exact edge occupation is 1/2, whereas the Boltzmann edge approximation gives 1. An integrated DOS calculation determines the actual carrier concentration.

questions.prompt: Which mathematical step remains valid when Boltzmann statistics fail?
questions.hint: Think of the DOS and occupation separately.
questions.answer: Counting states by integrating g(E)f(E) remains valid within the chosen band model. The exact FD occupation replaces the exponential approximation.

title: Band energy and potential
heading: An electron’s negative charge reverses the potential-to-energy sign
problem: why rising electrostatic potential bends electron bands downward
explanation: Band diagrams track electron energy; voltmeters track differences in electrostatic potential or electrochemical conditions. If material parameters are uniform, a local electrostatic potential ψ shifts an electron’s potential energy by −qψ. Thus EC(x) = EC0 − qψ(x), and EV shifts by the same amount when the bandgap remains fixed.

The electric field is Efield = −dψ/dx in one dimension. With EC measured in joules, Efield = (1/q)dEC/dx. A conduction electron experiences force −qEfield, while a hole experiences +qEfield. If energies are plotted numerically in eV, a one-volt potential increase lowers an electron band energy by one eV; keep the unit conversion explicit in derivatives.

A flat equilibrium Fermi level can coexist with curved EC and EV. Carrier concentration gradients then accompany the electrostatic field, and drift and diffusion balance to give zero net equilibrium current. Band bending alone does not establish a current without occupancy and boundary conditions.

Check the horizontal axis before interpreting a curve. In an energy-versus-position diagram, the band-edge slope gives an electric field. In an energy-versus-wave-vector diagram, k is wave vector and ℏk is crystal momentum, where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. The slope gives group velocity, and the curvature gives inverse effective mass near a parabolic band edge. The same vertical energy units support two different physical readings.

Read a band diagram in three passes. First, take vertical energy differences at one position to find populations. Second, follow the spatial slope of a band edge to find the electric field. Third, use its curvature, together with permittivity and boundary conditions, to infer space charge. Across an equilibrium silicon PN junction, one flat EF can coexist with different EC − EF separations in the two neutral bulks, preserving their different carrier concentrations.
example: Moving from ψ = 0 to ψ = +0.2 V lowers electron potential energy by 0.2 eV. The associated field direction depends on which spatial direction has the increasing ψ.

questions.prompt: If EC slopes upward with increasing x, which way does the electric field point?
questions.answer: The field points toward +x. An electron’s electrostatic force points toward −x.

The three panels use a positive uniform charge density and the boundary condition Efield(0) = 0. The field therefore rises linearly, and potential curves downward quadratically. Integration constants come from electrode potentials, symmetry or specified fields. Charge density alone determines curvature, rather than a unique absolute potential.

At an ideal sheet of free charge σ, the normal displacement jump is D2,n − D1,n = σ, with D = εEfield and σ in C/m². A sheet differs from a volume distribution: it gives a field discontinuity. Boundary conditions at material interfaces and contacts are essential for junction and MOS calculations; consistent length units prevent large permittivity and concentration conversion errors.

Mobile carriers screen a small electrostatic disturbance over a characteristic distance. In a uniform nondegenerate n-type bulk dominated by electrons of equilibrium concentration n0, the linear-response Debye length is LD = √[εkBT/(q²n0)]. The carrier density responds to potential while Poisson’s equation links that response to curvature, smoothing the transition around an abrupt doping change. This bulk screening length depends on the carrier population and temperature; a transistor’s channel scale length instead follows its geometry and electrostatic boundary conditions.
example: For a uniformly charged slab with Efield(0) = 0, doubling slab thickness at fixed ρ doubles the outer-edge field and quadruples the magnitude of the potential drop from that boundary.

questions.prompt: What information is still missing after integrating Poisson’s equation twice?
questions.answer: Two boundary conditions are required in one dimension, such as potentials at two contacts or one reference potential plus a specified field.

title: Drift, mobility and conductivity
heading: Scattering converts field acceleration into an average drift velocity
problem: how carrier sign and scattering determine drift current
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" viewBox="0 0 900 500"><title id="title">Scattering converts field acceleration into an average drift velocity</title><desc id="desc">Figure showing how carrier sign and scattering determine drift current.</desc><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z" fill="#17343d"/></marker></defs><rect width="900" height="500" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui,sans-serif"><text x="450" y="40" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">Electron velocity and conventional current have opposite signs</text><line x1="200" y1="115" x2="710" y2="115" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="450" y="90" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Electric field E</text><circle cx="450" cy="225" r="17" fill="#176a70" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450" y="232" fill="white" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle">−</text><line x1="420" y1="225" x2="185" y2="225" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="295" y="270" fill="#176a70" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Electron drift velocity</text><line x1="480" y1="225" x2="715" y2="225" stroke="#b04745" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="615" y="270" fill="#b04745" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Electron current Jn</text><text x="450" y="350" fill="#17343d" font-size="25" text-anchor="middle">vn = −μn E     Jn = (−q)n vn = qnμn E</text><text x="450" y="420" fill="#17343d" font-size="25" text-anchor="middle">σ = q(nμn + pμp)     [S/m]</text><text x="450" y="470" fill="#627b82" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle">Low-field drift; holes have positive charge and drift along E.</text></g></svg>
explanation: An electric field changes carrier momentum between scattering events. In the low-field regime, electron drift velocity is vn = −μnEfield and hole drift velocity is vp = +μpEfield. Positive mobilities μn and μp have units m²/(V·s), or cm²/(V·s) with consistent concentrations and lengths. Thermal motion can be rapid even when its directional average vanishes.

Conventional current includes the charge sign: Jn,drift = qnμnEfield and Jp,drift = qpμpEfield. Both drift currents point along the electric field. Total conductivity is σ = q(nμn + pμp), in S/m in SI. In a simple isotropic relaxation-time model, μ = qτm/m*, where τm is a momentum-relaxation time and m* is the transport mass.

Lattice vibrations, ionized impurities, interfaces and other processes scatter carriers. Their relative importance changes with temperature, doping and structure, so a single temperature trend for mobility is insufficient. At strong fields, carrier heating and scattering make average drift speed depart from μE and tend toward a material-dependent saturation scale. This microscopic velocity saturation differs from a MOSFET’s channel-electrostatic current saturation, although both can influence its I–V curve.

Track the carrier count and the ease of motion separately when temperature changes. In intrinsic material, warming can create many more electron–hole pairs, raising conductivity even while phonon scattering reduces mobility. In an extrinsic range with nearly fully ionized dopants, the carrier count changes relatively little, so the mobility decrease can dominate. The trend follows σ = q(nμn + pμp) with all four quantities evaluated in the same regime.

A ball-and-obstacles picture helps visualize momentum becoming randomized between field-driven accelerations. In a crystal, conduction states are extended electron waves. Lattice vibrations, charged impurities and disorder scatter those states; the perfectly periodic lattice is already incorporated in the band structure and effective mass. This sets the useful scope of the mechanical picture.
example: If electron density stays fixed while a change in scattering halves μn, the electron contribution to conductivity halves. A simultaneous change in density would need to be counted separately.

questions.prompt: Which way is the conventional electron drift current relative to electron drift velocity?
questions.answer: They point in opposite directions. Electrons drift against the field, while their conventional drift current points along it.

title: Diffusion and the Einstein relation
heading: Particle diffusion and electrical current carry different signs
problem: how a concentration gradient moves electrons even without an applied field
explanation: Random microscopic motion produces a net particle flow from higher to lower concentration. For electrons in one dimension, Fick’s law is Γn = −Dn dn/dx, where Γn is particle flux in m⁻²s⁻¹ and Dn is the diffusion coefficient in m²/s. Multiplying by electron charge gives conventional diffusion current Jn,diff = +qDn dn/dx. The arrows in the figure point in opposite directions because electron charge is negative.

For holes, Γp = −Dp dp/dx and Jp,diff = −qDp dp/dx. Including drift gives Jn = qμnnEfield + qDn dn/dx and Jp = qμppEfield − qDp dp/dx. These current densities are in A/m² when SI units are used throughout. A concentration gradient and a field can oppose each other, including the zero-current balance inside an equilibrium junction.

For nondegenerate carriers at uniform temperature in the low-field drift–diffusion model, Dn/μn = Dp/μp = kBT/q = VT. VT is the thermal voltage, about 25.9 mV at 300 K. The Einstein relation connects fluctuation-driven spreading to field-driven response. Degeneracy or hot carriers require a generalized relation.
example: At 300 K, an illustrative mobility of 800 cm²/(V·s) corresponds to D ≈ 20.7 cm²/s through D = μVT. Keep the centimetre units in both μ and D, or convert both to SI.

questions.prompt: If electron concentration decreases toward +x, which way do electron diffusion flux and current point?
questions.hint: Evaluate dn/dx, then include electron charge.
questions.answer: The gradient is negative, so Γn points toward +x and Jn,diff points toward −x.

questions.prompt: Why do D/μ and kBT/q have compatible units?
questions.answer: The mobility ratio has units V; energy divided by charge is also a volt.

title: Quasi-Fermi levels
heading: Separate chemical potentials describe injected electrons and holes
problem: how an electron–hole population above equilibrium appears as a level splitting
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" viewBox="0 0 900 500"><title id="title">Separate chemical potentials describe injected electrons and holes</title><desc id="desc">Figure showing how an electron–hole population above equilibrium appears as a level splitting.</desc><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z" fill="#17343d"/></marker></defs><rect width="900" height="500" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui,sans-serif"><text x="450" y="35" fill="#17343d" font-size="22" text-anchor="middle">Separate carrier populations need separate quasi-Fermi levels</text><line x1="140" y1="110" x2="700" y2="110" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="3"/><text x="730" y="117" fill="#176a70" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">EC</text><line x1="140" y1="190" x2="700" y2="190" stroke="#b04745" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><text x="730" y="197" fill="#b04745" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">EFn</text><line x1="140" y1="270" x2="700" y2="270" stroke="#9a6a15" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><text x="730" y="277" fill="#9a6a15" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">EFp</text><line x1="140" y1="355" x2="700" y2="355" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="3"/><text x="730" y="362" fill="#176a70" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">EV</text><line x1="435" y1="260" x2="435" y2="200" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="460" y="235" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="start">EFn − EFp</text><text x="450" y="420" fill="#17343d" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle">np = ni² exp[(EFn − EFp)/kBT]</text><text x="450" y="470" fill="#627b82" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle">Local quasi-equilibrium, common temperature, nondegenerate bands.</text></g></svg>
explanation: An operating junction can have electrons and holes that each relax internally while remaining out of mutual equilibrium. Their populations can then be described by electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels EFn and EFp. In a nondegenerate local model, n = NC exp[−(EC − EFn)/(kBT)] and p = NV exp[−(EFp − EV)/(kBT)]. All energies use the same reference.

Multiplication gives np = ni² exp[(EFn − EFp)/(kBT)]. At equilibrium EFn = EFp = EF and the ordinary mass-action product returns. A positive splitting EFn − EFp corresponds to a carrier product above equilibrium. The splitting is an energy; dividing by q expresses its voltage equivalent.

Spatial quasi-Fermi-level gradients describe the electrochemical driving forces for current under the transport assumptions. In an ideal forward-biased junction, the edge populations can be related to an applied voltage through an approximately qV splitting. Contact resistance, recombination and high injection can change this relationship, so the terminal voltage and every local splitting need not coincide.
example: A splitting of kBT gives np = e·ni² in the nondegenerate local model. This specifies the product; neutrality, injection conditions and boundary conditions are needed to find n and p individually.

questions.prompt: What does a single flat Fermi level imply about the equilibrium carrier product?
questions.answer: The exponential becomes one, giving np = ni² within the nondegenerate equilibrium model.

title: Continuity and lifetime
heading: Carrier conservation combines transport with generation and recombination
problem: how a small semiconductor region gains and loses electrons
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" viewBox="0 0 900 500"><title id="title">Carrier conservation combines transport with generation and recombination</title><desc id="desc">Figure showing how a small semiconductor region gains and loses electrons.</desc><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z" fill="#17343d"/></marker></defs><rect width="900" height="500" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui,sans-serif"><text x="450" y="35" fill="#17343d" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">A carrier inventory balances flow, generation and loss</text><rect x="285" y="120" width="330" height="210" rx="5" fill="#edf4f1" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="232.0" fill="#17343d" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">Electrons n × volume</text><line x1="60" y1="220" x2="275" y2="220" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="160" y="185" fill="#176a70" font-size="19" text-anchor="middle">Particle inflow</text><line x1="625" y1="220" x2="835" y2="220" stroke="#b04745" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="735" y="185" fill="#b04745" font-size="19" text-anchor="middle">Particle outflow</text><line x1="450" y1="65" x2="450" y2="110" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="480" y="90" fill="#176a70" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">G</text><line x1="450" y1="340" x2="450" y2="385" stroke="#b04745" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="480" y="370" fill="#b04745" font-size="20" text-anchor="start">R</text><text x="450" y="425" fill="#17343d" font-size="25" text-anchor="middle">∂n/∂t = (1/q)∇·Jn + G − R</text><text x="450" y="475" fill="#627b82" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle">Jn is conventional electron current; particle flux Γn = −Jn/q.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A carrier population changes through transport across its boundary, generation and recombination. Because electron particle flux is Γn = −Jn/q, electron conservation gives ∂n/∂t = (1/q)∇·Jn + G − R. Hole conservation gives ∂p/∂t = −(1/q)∇·Jp + G − R. G and R count created or removed electron–hole pairs per volume per second; current density is conventional electrical current.

For a spatially uniform excess minority population in low-level injection, a useful linear approximation is excess net recombination Δn/τn. After an external optical pulse ends, with no carrier flow, dΔn/dt = −Δn/τn and Δn(t) = Δn(0)exp(−t/τn). The lifetime τn is an effective time constant, in seconds, for the specified material, injection regime and mechanisms.

With a constant additional uniform generation rate Gext, the same model gives dΔn/dt = Gext − Δn/τn and steady excess Δn = Gextτn. Traps, radiative processes, Auger recombination and surfaces can make the effective lifetime depend on density or position. Boundary extraction and diffusion must be restored when the sample is nonuniform.

In a uniform one-dimensional steady device, define U = R − G as the net recombination rate per volume. The continuity equations give dJn/dx = qU and dJp/dx = −qU, so d(Jn + Jp)/dx = 0. Recombination changes how the total current is divided between electrons and holes while their sum remains constant. Integrating qU over a length gives a current density: C × m⁻³s⁻¹ × m = A/m².
example: After two lifetimes in the uniform pulse-decay model, the excess population is e⁻² ≈ 13.5% of its initial value. This fraction follows from the model rather than from a specific device geometry.

questions.prompt: Why do electron and hole continuity equations have opposite current-divergence signs?
questions.hint: Write particle flux as electrical current divided by carrier charge.
questions.answer: Electron charge is −q while hole charge is +q. Converting each conventional current to particle flux gives opposite signs.

questions.prompt: If uniform generation doubles at fixed lifetime, what happens to steady excess density?
questions.answer: The steady excess density doubles while the same low-injection, uniform model remains applicable.

title: Minority-carrier diffusion
heading: A diffusion length compares spreading with recombination
problem: why an injected minority population decays away from a junction
explanation: A forward-biased junction injects minority carriers into the adjacent quasi-neutral material. Let u measure distance away from the injecting edge into a p-type region, and let Δn(u) = n(u) − np0 be excess minority-electron concentration. With negligible electric field, uniform Dn and low-injection lifetime τn, steady continuity becomes Dn d²Δn/du² − Δn/τn = 0.

For a semi-infinite region with Δn(0) fixed by injection and Δn → 0 far away, the solution is Δn(u) = Δn(0)exp(−u/Ln), where Ln = √(Dnτn). Ln has units of length and is the distance over which the excess concentration falls by a factor e in this particular geometry. It compares the time available before recombination with the rate of diffusive spreading.

An actual contact at finite distance, a recombining surface, a nonuniform field or high injection changes the boundary-value problem. The exponential profile should therefore be tied to its assumptions. Electron particle flux travels down this profile; its conventional diffusion current has the opposite direction. A junction’s terminal current includes the corresponding hole contribution as well.

For a switching calculation, specify an initial concentration profile and a condition at each boundary before evolving the diffusion equation. A recombining contact can fix one end near its equilibrium concentration; the external circuit can set a flux or gradient at the depletion edge. Reverse bias can produce a negative excess Δn while the total density n = np0 + Δn stays nonnegative. The admissible lower bound is Δn ≥ −np0, and the boundary model must follow the operating regime.
example: If lifetime increases by a factor of nine while Dn stays fixed, Ln increases by a factor of three. The profile extends farther from the injecting edge before reaching the same normalized concentration.

questions.prompt: What happens to the normalized concentration at u = Ln?
questions.answer: It is e⁻¹, approximately 0.368 of its edge value.

questions.prompt: Why can a nearby extracting contact change the exponential profile?
questions.answer: The semi-infinite solution requires the excess to vanish only far away. A finite contact imposes a different condition at a finite distance, so the full solution must satisfy that condition.

explanation: Joining p-type and n-type material creates concentration gradients. Initial diffusion uncovers negative ionized acceptors on the p side and positive ionized donors on the n side. Their electric field points from n toward p and opposes further majority-carrier diffusion. At equilibrium a common Fermi level and balanced drift and diffusion accompany this built-in field.

For an abrupt junction in the depletion approximation, mobile charge is neglected inside widths xp and xn. Charge neutrality per area requires NAxp = NDxn. The total depleted width is W = xp + xn = √{[2εs(Vbi − V)/q](1/NA + 1/ND)}, where εs is semiconductor permittivity, V is positive for forward bias, and Vbi is the equilibrium built-in potential. Width and concentration units must be consistent.

For fully ionized nondegenerate uniform sides, Vbi = VT ln(NAND/ni²). Forward bias reduces the depletion potential Vbi − V; reverse bias increases it. The approximation applies while a depleted region exists and effects such as high injection, tunneling, breakdown and strong grading can be neglected. The less heavily doped side occupies more of W.
example: If NA = 4ND, charge balance gives xn = 4xp: the more lightly doped n side has four times the depleted width. At fixed doping, doubling the depletion potential increases W by √2.

questions.prompt: Why does a built-in field coexist with zero net equilibrium current?
questions.answer: The field-driven current balances the concentration-gradient-driven current for each carrier type at thermal equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Which side holds most of the depletion width in a strongly one-sided junction?
questions.answer: The lower-doped side needs a larger width to supply the same magnitude of uncovered ion charge.

title: PN diode injection
heading: Forward bias changes minority boundary populations exponentially
problem: how reducing the junction barrier drives minority-carrier current
explanation: A PN diode conducts by changing the carrier populations at the edges of its depletion region. Under ideal nondegenerate low-level injection, forward voltage V raises each minority edge concentration by exp(V/VT), with VT = kBT/q. Low-level injection means the excess minority density remains small compared with the equilibrium majority density, so the majority population changes little. Carriers then diffuse into the quasi-neutral regions and recombine or reach a contact.

For long uniform quasi-neutral regions and negligible depletion-region recombination, the ideal result is I = Is[exp(V/VT) − 1]. The saturation scale is Is = qA ni²[Dn/(LnNA) + Dp/(LpND)], where A is junction area, Dn and Dp are minority diffusion coefficients, and Ln and Lp are diffusion lengths. Both carrier contributions add to the terminal current. SI concentrations, lengths and diffusivities make Is an ampere.

The depletion edges provide a convenient bridge from voltage to current. Forward bias first sets the minority concentrations at those edges. The diffusion equation then gives their profiles in the nearly neutral regions, and each edge slope gives a minority diffusion current. Adding the electron and hole contributions gives the terminal current under the stated ideal assumptions. With appreciable series resistance Rs, use the local junction voltage Vj = Vterminal − IRs in the injection relation.

The exponential law describes a model with specified boundaries and transport. In high injection, excess carrier density becomes comparable to or exceeds the original majority density, so both populations change substantially. Depletion-region recombination, series resistance, leakage and breakdown also alter the response. Forward current stores excess minority charge; changing that charge during switching links the static law to lifetime and transient continuity.
example: In the ideal exponential region, increasing forward voltage by VT ln 3 multiplies the exp(V/VT) term by three. The current ratio approaches three only when that term is much larger than one.

questions.prompt: Why is the subtraction of one present?
questions.hint: Evaluate the law at zero terminal voltage.
questions.answer: It gives I = 0 at V = 0, representing the balance between equilibrium opposing carrier flows.

questions.prompt: What extra physical quantity matters during turn-off after forward conduction?
questions.hint: Think about carriers already injected into quasi-neutral material.
questions.answer: Stored excess minority charge must recombine or be extracted; the static I–V curve alone does not describe that transient.

heading: A strong reverse field can open a band-to-band quantum path
problem: how a sufficiently narrow forbidden region permits interband tunneling

explanation: A heavily doped reverse-biased junction can develop a large electric field over a short distance. Band bending can then place occupied valence states on one side at energies matching empty conduction states on the other. An electron can tunnel between these states through the forbidden region, creating a conduction electron and a valence hole.

The probability depends on the barrier shape, bandgap, carrier masses and allowed transitions. A semiclassical one-dimensional guide is transmission proportional to exp[−2∫κ(x)dx], where κ is an inverse decay length in the classically forbidden region. Narrowing that region can strongly increase tunneling. The figure is an energy-versus-position schematic, rather than a literal particle trajectory.

A local constant-field estimate for the band-to-band tunneling distance is ℓtun ≈ Eg/(q|Efield|), with Eg in joules and |Efield| in V/m. The electric field must shift a band energy by roughly one bandgap across that distance. This is the forbidden interval relevant to the transition; a nonuniform junction requires its actual band profile and may have a much wider total depletion region.

Band-to-band tunneling and impact-ionization avalanche are distinct reverse-current mechanisms. Avalanche involves energetic carriers generating additional pairs through collisions; tunneling accesses states quantum mechanically across a barrier. Which mechanism dominates depends on field, doping, band structure and temperature. The ordinary ideal Shockley law excludes both breakdown mechanisms.
example: Reducing a forbidden-region width while leaving a comparable decay constant κ increases transmission exponentially in the simple barrier approximation. Exact device predictions require the actual band profile and material model.

questions.prompt: Why can narrowing a barrier matter even if its peak height stays similar?
questions.answer: A smaller width reduces ∫κdx, so the exponential attenuation decreases and transmission rises.

title: Work functions and affinity

explanation: Before joining materials, a common vacuum reference helps organize their electron energies. Write qΦm = Evac − EFm for the metal work-function energy and qΦs = Evac − EFs for the semiconductor work-function energy. Electron affinity is qχ = Evac − EC. Here Φ and χ are expressed as volt-equivalent quantities and q times them is energy; the same numerical values are often quoted in eV for an electron.

For an ideal clean metal–n-semiconductor interface without an additional interface dipole, the Schottky–Mott electron barrier is φBn = Φm − χ. The semiconductor work function additionally depends on EF relative to EC, so doping can change Φs without changing electron affinity in the simple rigid-band model. Real interfaces can depart strongly from this ideal barrier prediction.

Build a contact diagram in stages. Separate materials can each be in equilibrium with their own chemical potential. Connecting them through a conducting wire allows charge to redistribute and establishes a common equilibrium Fermi level, while facing surfaces separated by a gap can hold capacitor-like charge. Bringing the surfaces into physical contact then introduces the interface’s bonding, states and dipole. Follow the common energy reference and the electrostatic shifts through each stage.

The same bookkeeping enters MOS flat-band voltage. In an ideal charge-free oxide, VFB = Φg − Φs using consistent voltage units. A fixed oxide sheet charge Qox′ adds a term −Qox′/Cox′ in the elementary model. Zero applied bias establishes equilibrium, but flat semiconductor bands occur at Vg = VFB and therefore can require a nonzero gate voltage.
example: Two gates with different work functions on the same ideal semiconductor require different flat-band gate voltages even when oxide thickness is unchanged. Their oxide capacitance can be identical while their C–V curves are shifted horizontally.

questions.prompt: Why does electron affinity stop at EC rather than EF?
questions.hint: Compare the two definitions in the figure.
questions.answer: Affinity references the conduction-band edge. Work function references the chemical potential and consequently also depends on EF’s location relative to that edge.

questions.prompt: Does zero applied gate bias guarantee flat bands?
questions.answer: Flat bands require the applied voltage to match VFB. A work-function difference or oxide charge can make VFB nonzero.

explanation: Every device needs contacts, and a metal–semiconductor interface can either limit transport or serve as a nearly transparent connection. A Schottky barrier presents an energy barrier to a majority-carrier population. Its rectifying behavior depends on the barrier height, depletion width, applied bias and transport mechanism. Band bending is therefore part of the contact problem, even when the bulk semiconductor is neutral.

An ohmic contact has a sufficiently low, approximately linear voltage–current relation over its intended operating range. One route is a small effective majority-carrier barrier. Another is heavy contact-region doping that narrows the barrier enough for substantial tunneling. The contact can then be conductive even though a barrier remains in the band diagram.

The differential specific contact resistivity can be written ρc = dV/dJ near a stated bias, with units Ω·m². Actual contact resistance also depends on area and current spreading. Interface states, interfacial layers, processing and polarity matter. A generic metal choice or a work-function sketch alone does not establish a reliably ohmic fabricated contact.
example: For a uniform ideal contact with the same ρc, doubling contact area halves its lumped differential resistance ρc/A. Real layouts can depart from this area scaling when current crowding limits the effective transfer area.

questions.prompt: How can increasing semiconductor doping improve a contact without eliminating the barrier height?
questions.answer: Higher doping can narrow the depleted barrier, making tunneling more probable and reducing contact resistance.

title: Interface states and pinning
heading: Interfacial charge can weaken metal work-function control
problem: how interface states change the sensitivity of a contact barrier
explanation: An ideal work-function calculation can fail when the interface contains electronic states and dipoles. Defects, bonding changes and metal-induced gap states can exchange charge with the adjoining materials. This redistribution shifts the electrostatic potential across the interface and changes the relationship between metal work function and semiconductor barrier height.

A useful empirical sensitivity is S = dφBn/dΦm, with barrier and work-function quantities expressed in the same voltage units. The ideal Schottky–Mott limit has S near one. Strong Fermi-level pinning gives a much smaller sensitivity: changing the metal has a weaker effect on the barrier. The figure compares slopes rather than assigning a universal pinned energy.

Pinning strength depends on the actual material pair, surface preparation, interfacial layers and processing. An interface-state density is commonly quoted per area per energy, such as cm⁻²eV⁻¹; its electrostatic effect also depends on occupation. Depinning strategies therefore require an interface model and measurement, rather than a work-function change alone.

An interface with many available electronic states can exchange substantial charge through a comparatively small change in occupation energy. That charge helps set the local potential and can make the barrier less sensitive to the adjoining metal’s work function. Atomic bonding dipoles and the bias-dependent occupation of interface states contribute through different microscopic mechanisms, so a useful interface model identifies both.
example: If a measured contact family has S = 0.15, a work-function change of 0.4 V would correspond to about 0.06 V of barrier change within that local linear fit. The fit is specific to that family and range.

questions.prompt: What does a nearly horizontal barrier-versus-work-function curve indicate?
questions.answer: The barrier is weakly sensitive to the chosen metal work function, consistent with strong pinning in that contact family.

explanation: A contact barrier filters carrier energies. Thermionic emission uses carriers with sufficient thermal energy to pass over its top. In a simple ideal Schottky model, the thermionic current scale has a strong factor exp[−qφB/(kBT)], with barrier voltage φB and temperature T. The prefactor depends on the band structure and emission model.

Field emission tunnels through a sufficiently thin barrier from energies close to the occupied carrier supply. Thermionic-field emission combines thermal access to elevated energies with tunneling through the remaining barrier. The three arrows separate energy routes; they do not represent classical motion through a forbidden region. Doping, electric field and temperature help select the dominant route.

A depletion width can shrink with increasing doping or bias, making tunneling important even when a barrier height remains. Conversely, a wide barrier can suppress tunneling so that thermal activation dominates. Interpreting a measured I–V curve therefore benefits from temperature dependence, doping information and a consistent barrier profile, rather than fitting every contact to one exponential law.
example: For thermionic-dominated transport at fixed barrier and a suitable prefactor model, raising temperature increases the fraction of carriers able to reach the barrier top. A tunneling-dominated contact can show a much weaker thermal activation.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes thermionic-field emission from pure thermionic emission?
questions.hint: Identify the last part of the route.
questions.answer: Carriers first gain thermal energy but still tunnel through a remaining forbidden region; pure thermionic carriers pass over the barrier top.

title: Image-force barrier lowering
heading: A metal’s polarization modifies a nearby carrier barrier
problem: how a field and an attractive image interaction lower a classical barrier
explanation: A carrier near an ideal conducting plane polarizes the conductor. In the classical planar model, an electron at distance x in a dielectric of permittivity ε has image interaction energy Uim(x) = −q²/(16πεx). The factor includes the work of building the induced charge distribution. It is an attractive energy correction, measured in joules in SI.

For a positive field magnitude F that lowers the outward barrier, model its energy as U(x) = qφB − qFx − q²/(16πεx). The maximum occurs at xm = √[q/(16πεF)]. Its reduction relative to the unrounded interface barrier is ΔU = qΔφ, where Δφ = √[qF/(4πε)] in volts. Increasing F by four therefore doubles the classical barrier-lowering voltage.

This model assumes an ideal planar metal, a locally uniform field and a continuum dielectric response. Its divergence as x approaches zero signals the failure of that continuum description at atomic distances. Nonplanar contacts, two-dimensional screening and interface chemistry require more detailed models. Image-force lowering is one correction to contact transport, rather than a replacement for the full barrier profile.
example: A fourfold increase in field magnitude moves xm inward by a factor of two and doubles Δφ in this planar model. Both trends make the barrier easier to cross, while the model’s microscopic limits remain important.

questions.prompt: Why should the classical formula not be extrapolated to x = 0?
questions.hint: Inspect its inverse-distance behavior and underlying material model.
questions.answer: The continuum ideal-plane approximation gives a divergent interaction. Atomic structure, screening and interface bonding determine the near-interface physics there.

title: Quantum wells and subbands
heading: Confinement quantizes one direction while leaving transport states in others
problem: how a confined direction produces discrete energy levels
explanation: When a carrier is confined over a short distance, its wavefunction and boundary conditions determine allowed energies. For an ideal infinite well from x = 0 to L with constant effective mass m*, the one-dimensional eigenstates are ψn(x) = √(2/L)sin(nπx/L) and En = n²π²ℏ²/(2m*L²), with integer n ≥ 1. ψ has units m⁻¹/² so that ∫|ψ|²dx = 1.

Picture the pressure wave in an organ pipe open at both ends: pressure nodes select its standing-wave modes. An electron in an ideal hard-wall well also obeys nodal boundary conditions. Fitting the same mode into a narrower well requires more spatial curvature and raises its kinetic energy. The pipe is a picture of allowed modes; the electronic potential and barrier conditions set the actual wavefunction.

The figure offsets each wavefunction by its energy level; its oscillation represents amplitude, not a classical particle path. A carrier confined in x but free in the other two directions has a sequence of subband edges En, with continuous in-plane kinetic energy above each edge. Each parabolic 2D subband adds its own DOS step, and FD occupation determines its sheet population.

A MOS inversion layer has an electrostatically shaped, finite confinement potential rather than an infinite rectangular well. Its subband energies, spatial charge centroid and self-consistent potential require a more appropriate Schrödinger–Poisson treatment. The ideal well isolates the size and mass scaling that helps interpret those device calculations.

A self-consistent MOS calculation closes a feedback loop. Begin with a trial potential, solve for confined wavefunctions and subband energies, and use their occupation to build the electron density. Each occupied mode contributes a density profile proportional to its |ψn(x)|², weighted by that subband’s sheet population. Poisson’s equation then updates the potential from mobile and fixed charge. Repeat until the potential and populations agree.
example: Halving L at fixed mass multiplies every ideal-well En by four. Doubling m* at fixed L halves the confinement energies. These ratios follow directly from the stated ideal model.

questions.prompt: Why is the lowest confined energy nonzero in an infinite well?
questions.hint: Use n = 1 and the boundary conditions.
questions.answer: A nonzero wavefunction that vanishes at both walls must vary spatially. Its curvature carries kinetic energy; a constant n = 0 function would be identically zero under these boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why is the carrier density of an occupied 2D subband a sheet density?
questions.answer: Confinement leaves two continuous transport directions, so state counting is per area. The confined wavefunction supplies the distribution normal to that area.

title: MOS C–V and response time
heading: Small-signal frequency and DC sweep history probe different carrier responses
problem: why one MOS structure can produce low-frequency, high-frequency and deep-depletion curves
explanation: A capacitance measurement asks how much gate charge changes for a small voltage change around a DC bias. Per unit area, C′ = dQg′/dVg and Cox′ = εox/tox. In an ideal MOS capacitor with a conductive gate, oxide and semiconductor differential capacitances are in series: 1/C′ = 1/Cox′ + 1/Cs′. Cs′ represents the semiconductor charge response, including whichever mobile and depletion components can follow the measurement.

At one bias point, the depletion and inversion charge responses share the same surface-potential change, so their differential contributions add within Cs′ when each population can respond. The oxide and that combined semiconductor response carry equal incremental gate charge in the ideal series description. This explains why the inversion response can change with frequency while the physical oxide capacitance stays the same.

For a p-type body, accumulation commonly gives C′ near Cox′. Depletion widens a space-charge region and lowers C′. In strong inversion with a sufficiently slow small signal and an available minority-carrier supply, inversion charge follows and capacitance rises toward Cox′. At high small-signal frequency the minority population cannot change appreciably, so the measured capacitance stays near the series combination with the maximum-depletion capacitance Cdep,max′ = εs/Wmax.

The DC sweep rate is a second timescale. A rapid move into inversion can leave too few minority carriers to establish the equilibrium inversion layer, extending depletion beyond Wmax and reducing capacitance below its high-frequency equilibrium minimum: deep depletion. Interface traps, series resistance and contact geometry add further responses. Always state bias history, AC frequency and how minority carriers are supplied when interpreting C–V.
example: Suppose a depletion-region semiconductor capacitance is equal to Cox′. Their series combination is C′ = Cox′/2. A later low-frequency inversion response can raise Cs′ substantially and move the measured C′ back toward Cox′.

questions.prompt: How do high-frequency inversion and deep depletion differ physically?
questions.hint: Separate a small AC perturbation from the establishment of the DC carrier population.
questions.answer: High-frequency equilibrium inversion has a DC inversion population that cannot follow the fast AC signal. Deep depletion lacks enough inversion charge even for the evolving DC bias, so depletion extends farther.

questions.prompt: Why can oxide capacitance stay unchanged while measured MOS capacitance falls?
questions.answer: The oxide remains the same, while a smaller semiconductor differential capacitance reduces the series total.

A doped polysilicon gate can instead develop a depleted region near the oxide under an appropriate bias. That region contains exposed ionized dopants and supports an electric field, adding voltage drop before the field reaches the oxide and semiconductor.

In a simple depletion approximation, the gate-region capacitance per area is Cpoly′ = εSi/Wpoly. Its series contribution gives 1/Ctotal′ = 1/Cpoly′ + 1/Cox′ + 1/Cs′. Wpoly is a bias-dependent gate depletion width in metres, and each C′ is in F/m². A smaller Cpoly′ lowers the incremental gate charge produced by a voltage change and weakens electrostatic control.

Gate depletion differs from depletion in the semiconductor body and from the finite centroid of quantum-confined inversion charge. All can introduce voltage drops, but they arise in different regions and require different models. A sufficiently conductive metal gate removes the particular finite-doped-polysilicon depletion term, while work-function and interface effects still remain.
example: If a simplified structure has Cpoly′ = Cox′ and an extremely large Cs′, its total capacitance is Cox′/2. With a highly conductive gate, the same oxide-limited structure would instead approach Cox′.

questions.prompt: Which physical region produces the extra series term in this lesson?
questions.hint: Locate the depleted layer above the oxide.
questions.answer: The finite-doped polysilicon gate itself develops a depleted region. The body depletion capacitance is a separate term below the oxide.

In a conceptual self-aligned gate-first process, a patterned gate shields the channel region while exposed regions receive source/drain implantation. The gate edge supplies the alignment reference, reducing the need to align an independent source/drain mask precisely to that edge.

Sidewall spacers establish an additional geometric offset for later processing. Isolation, gate dielectric formation, patterning, doping, activation and contacts all contribute to the resulting cross section. Implant straggle and subsequent thermal diffusion mean that an electrical junction edge is a concentration profile rather than an infinitely sharp mask edge.

Material purity, interface quality and repeatable processing are part of device behavior: they affect traps, mobility, leakage, contact resistance and variability. The diagram conveys the alignment principle. Specific modern technologies can use different gate ordering, replacement-gate steps and three-dimensional geometries, so a complete process flow must match the intended technology.
example: A wider sidewall spacer can increase the offset of a later source/drain implant from the gate edge. The final electrical overlap still depends on implantation and thermal evolution, so spacer width alone does not fix every junction dimension.

title: Parabolic and Dirac bands
heading: The dispersion law determines velocity and state counting
problem: how a linear band crossing differs from a parabolic band edge
explanation: An effective-mass parabola is one local band model. Near an ordinary parabolic minimum, E − E0 = ℏ²k²/(2m*) and group velocity grows with k. Near an ideal graphene Dirac point, the low-energy branches are approximately E± − ED = ±ℏvF|k|, where ED is the crossing energy and vF is a characteristic velocity. Wave vector k is measured relative to the relevant extremum or crossing.

Because velocity is (1/ℏ)∇kE, the ideal linear model has a nearly constant speed magnitude vF on each branch, with direction determined by k and branch. A constant parabolic effective mass obtained from a nonzero second derivative is therefore not the suitable starting model at the crossing. Real bands have limits to the linear approximation.

Dimensionality and dispersion together determine DOS. A two-dimensional parabolic band has constant DOS above its edge, whereas an ideal two-dimensional Dirac spectrum has DOS proportional to |E − ED|. A confined nanotube requires its own allowed circumferential wave vectors and subbands; its gap depends on structure. Semimetal band overlap and a zero-gap point crossing are distinct possible band arrangements.
example: In the ideal 2D Dirac model, moving twice as far in energy from ED doubles the DOS magnitude. The corresponding 2D parabolic-band DOS stays constant within one subband.

questions.prompt: Why is the 2D constant-DOS formula for a parabolic band unsuitable at an ideal Dirac point?
questions.answer: That formula assumes E − E0 proportional to k². A linear dispersion changes the relationship between k-space state count and energy, producing a DOS proportional to energy distance from the crossing.

explanation: The same minority-carrier physics appears in a bipolar transistor. In forward-active operation of an NPN device, the emitter–base junction is forward biased and the base–collector junction is reverse biased. Electrons injected from the n-type emitter become minority carriers in the p-type base. A sufficiently thin base allows many to diffuse to the collector depletion region, whose field sweeps them onward.

Some injected electrons recombine in the base, and hole injection into the emitter also contributes to base-current requirements. Using positive terminal-current magnitudes in the usual forward-active convention, IE = IC + IB. Define common-base gain α = IC/IE and common-emitter gain β = IC/IB; then β = α/(1 − α). These ratios summarize terminal behavior rather than replacing the transport and recombination model.

Injected minority charge is stored in the device. Switching conditions must change that charge as well as terminal voltage, so lifetime, diffusion distance and junction bias history affect speed. Deep saturation forward biases both junctions and can add stored charge. This gives context for comparing a majority-carrier Schottky contact with a minority-injecting PN structure under specified operating conditions.

Switching a minority-injecting junction also changes a stored concentration profile. The depletion-edge boundary can respond quickly to a changed bias while excess carriers farther into a quasi-neutral region remain. Those carriers leave through diffusion to contacts, field-assisted collection where a field is present, and recombination. The delay therefore depends on the spatial profile and the available removal paths as well as the applied voltage.
example: If an illustrative forward-active transistor has α = 0.98, its corresponding current ratio is β = 49. Achieving that ratio depends on injection efficiency, base transport and recombination, rather than on terminal algebra alone.

questions.prompt: Why does making the base thin relative to a minority diffusion length help collection?
questions.hint: Compare transit distance with recombination loss.
questions.answer: Injected electrons can reach the collector-side depletion region with a smaller chance of recombining in the base.

questions.prompt: What physical state must be tracked to predict switching after substantial injection?
questions.answer: The stored excess carrier distribution must be tracked or approximated. Terminal voltages alone do not specify how quickly that charge leaves.

explanation: Start with the physical question the material answers. Identify what the figure represents, where its boundaries are, which direction each axis increases and what each line or region means. Translate one visible feature into a sentence before reaching for an equation: for example, particles diffuse down a concentration gradient.

For each equation, name every symbol, its unit, its location in the figure and whether it is an input, a derived quantity or a boundary condition. Record the assumptions that make the relation valid. Check dimensions and a limiting case, such as zero field, zero excess generation, a very wide well or a fully ionized bulk. These checks connect the mathematical expression to a physical prediction.

A small-parameter limit gives an equation a physical check. First isolate a dimensionless quantity x, then use (1 + x)^a ≈ 1 + ax when |x| is much smaller than one. Keep the first-order term through the algebra: it may be the term that carries the measurable change. In a donor-occupation calculation, substituting a positive dimensionless exponential for the Fermi-energy dependence can turn the equation into a quadratic; select a physically positive root before taking its logarithm.

For an energy-axis calculation, kBT ln(NC/ND) has units of energy because NC/ND is dimensionless. Multiplying by another energy factor would give energy squared, which flags a dimensional inconsistency before plotting. Choosing EC as the common energy reference makes a graph of EF − EC particularly easy to interpret.

Then explain the same idea to an imagined learner using the figure as the reference. Pose a small change to one input and predict its consequence before calculating. If the prediction is unclear, turn that gap into a specific question to resolve from the source. Active reconstruction and a fresh example provide stronger evidence of understanding than recognition while rereading.
example: For D/μ = kBT/q, first identify diffusion coefficient and mobility. Their ratio has units volts, matching energy per charge. Then ask whether the nondegenerate, low-field, uniform-temperature assumptions hold before applying the relation to a highly injected contact.

questions.answer: Ask which measured or predicted feature the formula controls, which inputs can change it, and which boundary or approximation makes the relationship valid.
